summary: In Greek mythology, Byblis (Ancient Greek Βυβλίς; also Bublis) is the Milesian twin who loved her brother Caunus. Ovid's Metamorphoses makes her the warning exemplum of incestuous passion: rejected, she pursued him across Caria and Lycia until grief turned her tears into a spring. This atlas node is the daughter of Miletus (id byblis-miletus), not the Phoenician city Byblos as a primary figure.
etymology: Ancient Greek Byblís / Bublís (Βυβλίς). Folk tradition linked her name to the Phoenician city Byblos; the myth itself aetiologizes a spring near Miletus from her ceaseless weeping.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: Byblis was daughter of Miletus. Ancient authors name her mother variously as Tragasia daughter of Celaenus; Cyanee (Cyane) daughter of the river-god Maeander; or Eidothea daughter of King Eurytus of Caria. Her twin brother was Caunus. Nonnus instead makes Byblis, Caunus, and Miletus children of Asterius son of Minos — a rarer genealogy. This entry follows the Milesian twin of the incest-and-spring cycle.

sections.heading: Mythology
paragraphs: In Ovid she first tries to excuse her desire as natural, then writes Caunus a long letter citing divine incest as precedent. Disgusted, he flees. She tears her clothes, runs mad, and pursues him through Greece and Asia Minor until exhaustion and endless tears transform her into a spring.

Parthenius cites a version close to Ovid that ends with Byblis hanging herself by her girdle, and another in which Caunus initiates the passion and then leaves before he loses control; Byblis still hangs herself after a long search. Conon follows that Caunus-first strand. Antoninus Liberalis has her refuse other suitors and leap from a cliff; hamadryads save her, put her to sleep, and change her into a nymph. Nonnus reverses the chase: Caunus courts Byblis with a song of divine incest. All traditions mention a spring born of her tears; Pausanias knew the spring Biblis in Milesian land.

sections.heading: Reception
paragraphs: Stephanus of Byzantium records the belief that Phoenician Byblos took its name from Byblis. Early modern sculpture recycled the theme: Pierre Le Gros the Younger's inventive restoration of a fragmentary Amor and Psyche group as Caunus rejecting Byblis spawned drawings and marbles, notably Laurent Delvaux's versions. The story stands beside Myrrha as a classical incest exemplum in Ovid's warning register.
